course.title: Accounting and Finance Management
course.description: A plain-language course in money skills for everyday Ugandans and small business owners: budgeting, saving, borrowing, simple records, profit and planning. Finish each module check to unlock the next module. Progressive from absolute beginner to confident small-business money manager.

modules.title: Module 1: Money Basics
modules.description: Tell needs from wants, make a budget, and track where money goes.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: Income, expenses and where money goes
lessons.description: Know what comes in, what goes out, and the difference.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

By the end of this lesson you will be able to say clearly where your money comes from, where it goes, and whether you are saving or sliding into debt.

Why this matters

Many people feel that money “disappears” before the month ends. Usually it is not a mystery. It is a small number of expenses, a few forgotten ones and some small daily spends that add up. You cannot fix what you cannot see.

Step 1: Know your income

Income is all the money that comes to you: salary or wages, business income, support and gifts, investment income. Always plan with your take-home (net) income.

Step 2: Know your expenses

Group expenses into fixed (rent), variable (food, transport) and occasional (school fees, repairs). Track for at least two weeks.

Practice

List every source of income and every expense for the last seven days. Total both sides. Are you ahead, even, or behind?

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Needs, wants and spending choices
lessons.description: Separate essentials from nice-to-haves so choices become clearer.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will classify spending into needs and wants and use that classification to protect essentials when money is tight.

Needs vs wants

Needs are the things required for basic living and obligations (rent, staple food, school fees, medicine, essential transport). Wants improve comfort or status but can be delayed or reduced (new phone, frequent eating out, extra data bundles beyond what work requires).

Practical rule

When income falls or an emergency appears, protect needs first. Cut or postpone wants. This simple ranking prevents debt spirals.

Practice

Take your last seven days of expenses and mark each as Need or Want. Total the Want column. What is one Want you could reduce next week?

lessons.title: Lesson 1.3: Making a simple budget
lessons.description: Build a realistic monthly plan that matches real income.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will create a one-month budget that starts from real income and allocates money to needs, savings and wants in that order.

Simple budget steps

  1. Write your expected take-home income for the month.
  2. List fixed needs and their amounts.
  3. Estimate variable needs.
  4. Decide a small savings amount (even 5–10 % if possible).
  5. Allocate what remains to wants, or leave a buffer.
  6. Check that the total of all allocations does not exceed income.

Practice

Build a budget for next month on one page. Share the total income and the three largest expense lines with a trusted person for a reality check.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.4: Tracking your money
lessons.description: Turn the budget into a living tool by recording actual spending.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will keep a simple daily or weekly record that shows whether you are following the budget.

Methods that work

  • Notebook cash book (date, description, in, out, balance).
  • Phone notes or a simple spreadsheet.
  • Mobile-money statements reviewed weekly.

Review once a week. Adjust the next week’s plan if a category is overspending.

Practice

Start a tracking method today. Record every expense for the next three days and compare the total with your budget for those days.

modules.title: Module 2: Saving and Borrowing
modules.description: Build savings habits and borrow only when the numbers make sense.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Why and how to save
lessons.description: Start small, stay consistent, and protect the money.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will set a realistic savings goal and choose a safe place to keep the money.

Why save

Savings create a buffer for emergencies, fund planned goals (school fees, stock, tools) and reduce the need for expensive emergency borrowing.

How to start

Even small regular amounts matter. Automate if possible (standing order or mobile-money lock). Keep emergency savings separate from spending money.

Practice

Choose one savings goal and the amount you will set aside each week or month for the next three months. Write where the money will be kept.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Interest in plain words
lessons.description: Understand what you earn on savings and what you pay on loans.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will explain simple interest in everyday language and compare the cost of different loans.

Core idea

Interest is the price of money over time. When you save, the bank or SACCO may pay you interest. When you borrow, you pay interest. Always ask for the total amount you will repay, not only the monthly figure.

Practice

For a loan of UGX 500 000 repaid in six equal monthly instalments that total UGX 590 000, calculate the extra amount paid as interest/fees.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Borrowing wisely
lessons.description: Borrow only for productive or essential purposes and only when you can repay.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will decide whether a proposed loan is wise by checking purpose, cost and repayment capacity.

Three tests

  1. Purpose – will this loan increase income or solve a genuine essential need?
  2. Cost – what is the total amount to be repaid?
  3. Capacity – after essential living costs, is the instalment comfortably affordable?

Practice

Apply the three tests to any loan offer you have seen recently. Would you take it? Why or why not?

lessons.title: Lesson 2.4: Avoiding debt traps and scams
lessons.description: Recognise high-cost credit and common fraud patterns.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will spot warning signs of debt traps and common mobile-money or lending scams.

Warning signs

  • Pressure to borrow quickly.
  • Unclear or changing total cost.
  • Requests for your PIN or one-time password.
  • Promises of “free” money or guaranteed investment returns.
  • Lenders who discourage you from reading the terms.

Practice

Write two sentences you would use to refuse a pushy loan offer or a suspicious mobile-money request.

lessons.title: Module 2 review and assessment
lessons.description: Module check. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 2 assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: A key reason to save is:
To increase spending on wants immediately
*To build a buffer for emergencies and planned goals
To avoid ever earning income
To impress friends only
explain: Savings create resilience and fund goals.
level: 1

Q: Interest on a loan is:
Money the lender pays you for free
*The cost you pay for using the lender’s money over time
Always zero
Only charged on savings
explain: Borrowers pay for the use of money.
level: 1

Q: When comparing loans you should look at:
Only the monthly instalment
*The total amount to be repaid and whether you can afford it
Only the colour of the lender’s logo
Only the first month’s payment
explain: Total cost and capacity matter most.
level: 2

Q: Borrowing to buy stock that you can sell at a profit is usually:
Always a trap
*A potentially productive use of credit if the numbers work
Illegal
Worse than borrowing for a party
explain: Productive purpose plus capacity can justify borrowing.
level: 2

Q: Sharing your mobile-money PIN with someone who calls claiming to be support is:
Safe if they sound official
*A common scam technique – never share your PIN
Required by law
Only risky for large amounts
explain: PINs must stay private.
level: 1

Q: A debt trap often involves:
Clear terms and low pressure
*High cost, pressure to borrow more, and difficulty escaping the cycle
Only government loans
Interest-free family support
explain: Traps keep people in permanent expensive debt.
level: 2

Q: Keeping emergency savings separate from daily spending money helps because:
It earns higher interest automatically
*It reduces the chance of spending the buffer on wants
It is required by every bank
It eliminates all risk
explain: Separation protects the buffer.
level: 2

Q: Before taking any loan you should be able to answer:
Only the interest rate percentage
*Purpose, total cost and whether repayments fit your budget
Only the lender’s name
How to hide the loan from family
explain: Purpose, cost and capacity are the three tests.
level: 1

Q: Regular small savings usually beat:
Occasional large deposits only when money is left over
*Irregular saving that depends on leftover cash
Never saving
Both of the above
explain: Consistency compounds.
level: 2

Q: If a lender discourages you from reading the full terms you should:
Sign immediately
*Treat it as a warning sign and walk away or get independent advice
Share your ID photos on social media
Borrow twice as much
explain: Transparency is non-negotiable.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 3: Simple Record Keeping
modules.description: Keep clear records that separate business and personal money.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.1: Why records matter
lessons.description: See how good records reduce stress and support better decisions.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will explain three concrete benefits of keeping simple written records.

Benefits

  • You know whether the business is making or losing money.
  • You can answer questions from partners, lenders or tax authorities with confidence.
  • You reduce arguments and forgotten debts.

Practice

List one decision you made in the last month that would have been easier with better records.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.2: The cash book
lessons.description: Record every inflow and outflow in one place.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will keep a basic cash book with date, description, money in, money out and running balance.

Simple format

Date | Details | In | Out | Balance. Update it on the same day as the transaction when possible. Reconcile weekly with mobile-money or bank balances.

Practice

Start a cash book for the next seven days for either personal or business money.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.3: Keeping business and personal money apart
lessons.description: Avoid mixing so that profit becomes visible.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will set up a practical separation between business and personal funds.

Why separation matters

When money is mixed, it is almost impossible to know whether the business is healthy. Pay yourself a fixed “salary” or drawings and record it. Keep a separate mobile-money line or wallet for the business if possible.

Practice

Decide one concrete step you will take this month to reduce mixing of business and personal money.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.4: Credit, debts and stock
lessons.description: Track what others owe you, what you owe, and what stock you hold.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will keep simple lists of receivables, payables and stock so that cash and profit are not confused.

Three lists

  • Who owes you (customer name, amount, date, due date).
  • Who you owe (supplier, amount, due date).
  • Stock on hand (item, quantity, approximate value).

Practice

Write today’s lists for any credit sales, unpaid bills and main stock items you have.

modules.title: Module 4: Understanding Profit and Business Health
modules.description: Calculate profit, set prices and know when the business is healthy.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.1: Sales, costs and profit
lessons.description: Profit = Sales − Costs. Track both carefully.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will calculate a simple profit figure for a period and distinguish it from cash in the pocket.

Basic equation

Profit = Sales − All costs (including stock used, transport, airtime, wages, rent share, etc.). Cash on hand can be higher or lower than profit because of credit sales, stock purchases and timing.

Practice

Estimate last month’s sales and all costs for a small activity you know. Calculate approximate profit or loss.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.2: Pricing and margin
lessons.description: Set prices that cover costs and leave a sustainable margin.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will calculate a selling price that covers cost and delivers a target margin.

Simple approach

Know the full cost of the item or service (including a fair share of overheads). Decide the minimum margin you need. Selling price must cover cost + margin. Check what customers will actually pay.

Practice

Pick one product or service. Estimate full cost and a target margin percentage. Calculate the implied selling price.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.3: Break-even
lessons.description: Know how much you must sell to cover all costs.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will calculate a simple break-even sales level.

Idea

Break-even is the sales amount at which profit is zero. Below it you lose money; above it you make profit. For a simple case: Break-even sales = Fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio (or use units if costs are clear per unit).

Practice

Estimate monthly fixed costs for a small activity and the average profit contribution per unit or per UGX of sales. Approximate the break-even level.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.4: Profit, cash and business health
lessons.description: Judge health by profit, cash and customer trends together.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will look at profit, cash position and basic trends to form a balanced view of business health.

Three questions

  1. Is the activity profitable after all costs?
  2. Is there enough cash to meet obligations on time?
  3. Are sales and customer numbers stable or improving?

Practice

Answer the three questions for a business or side activity you know, using the best numbers you have.

lessons.title: Module 4 review and assessment
lessons.description: Module check. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 4 assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Profit is best described as:
Cash in the mobile-money wallet
*Sales minus all costs
Only the largest sale of the month
Total stock value
explain: Profit = Sales − Costs.
level: 1

Q: Cash on hand can differ from profit because of:
Only the weather
*Credit sales, stock purchases and timing differences
The colour of the cash book
Government policy only
explain: Timing and credit create differences.
level: 2

Q: A selling price should normally:
Ignore all costs
*Cover full cost and leave a sustainable margin
Be the lowest in the market at any cost
Equal the competitor’s price exactly
explain: Cost-plus sustainable margin is a practical starting point.
level: 1

Q: Break-even is the sales level at which:
Profit is maximised
*Profit is zero
Cash is infinite
All stock is sold
explain: Break-even = zero profit point.
level: 1

Q: Knowing break-even helps you:
Avoid all record keeping
*Understand how much you must sell to avoid losses
Set prices below cost forever
Ignore fixed costs
explain: It sets a clear minimum target.
level: 2

Q: Business health should be judged by:
Only the owner’s feelings
*Profit, cash position and basic sales/customer trends together
Only the number of social-media likes
Only the size of the shop
explain: Multiple indicators give a balanced view.
level: 1

Q: Margin is:
The same as total sales
*The difference between selling price and cost (often expressed as a percentage)
Only the rent amount
A type of loan
explain: Margin is the cushion above cost.
level: 1

Q: If sales are below break-even for several months the business is:
Definitely growing
*Likely losing money and needs action
Automatically profitable
Exempt from record keeping
explain: Prolonged operation below break-even destroys capital.
level: 2

Q: Including a fair share of overheads in product cost helps:
Understate true cost
*Set more realistic prices
Hide profit from partners
Increase tax automatically
explain: Full cost awareness improves pricing.
level: 2

Q: A business can show accounting profit yet still run out of cash if:
It never sells anything
*Customers pay slowly while the business must pay suppliers and expenses quickly
All sales are cash
It has no costs
explain: Timing of cash flows matters.
level: 2

modules.title: Module 5: Planning, Protecting and Growing
modules.description: Set goals, protect what you have, and plan the next stage of growth.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.1: Setting goals and a money plan
lessons.description: Turn hopes into dated, measurable targets.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will write two or three money goals that are specific, measurable and time-bound.

SMART enough

Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound. Example: “Save UGX 300 000 for school fees by 30 November by setting aside UGX 25 000 each week.”

Practice

Write one personal and one business (or side-activity) money goal in SMART form.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.2: Protecting what you have
lessons.description: Reduce the risk of sudden loss.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will list practical protection steps for cash, stock, tools and important records.

Practical protections

  • Secure storage and limited access to cash.
  • Basic insurance where affordable and relevant.
  • Backup of key records (digital + paper).
  • Diversifying income sources over time.
  • Avoiding concentrated risky bets with money you cannot afford to lose.

Practice

Identify the single biggest risk to your money or business right now and one action that would reduce it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.3: Making money grow
lessons.description: Reinvest profits and improve the business systematically.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will prioritise reinvestment options that improve profit or resilience.

Growth options

  • Restock faster-moving items.
  • Improve quality or customer experience that justifies better prices.
  • Reduce waste and leakage.
  • Add a complementary product or service.
  • Build skills that increase earning power.

Practice

Rank three possible uses of the next UGX 100 000 of profit and choose the one with the best expected return or risk reduction.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.4: Tax, honesty and your next steps
lessons.description: Stay on the right side of the rules and plan continuous improvement.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

You will recognise basic tax obligations that may apply and commit to honest records and continuous learning.

Key points

Tax rules depend on the size and type of activity. When in doubt, ask a qualified person or the relevant authority. Honest records protect you and make growth sustainable. Schedule a monthly money review.

Practice

Write three next actions you will take in the coming 30 days to improve your money management, based on this course.

lessons.title: Module 5 review and assessment
lessons.description: Final module check. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 5 assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.

Q: A useful money goal is:
“Become rich someday”
*Specific, measurable and time-bound
Secret from everyone including yourself
Only about spending more

level: 1

Q: Separating emergency savings from daily spending money is an example of:

*Protecting what you have
Avoiding all goals
Ignoring records
explain: Protection reduces the chance of losing the buffer.
level: 1

Q: Reinvesting profit into faster-moving stock is usually:
A way to hide money
*A practical growth step when demand is proven
Riskier than spending it all on wants
Only for large companies
explain: Capital put into proven demand can grow the business.
level: 2

Q: Honest records help with tax and with:
Avoiding all customers
*Building trust with partners and lenders
Increasing interest rates automatically
Eliminating the need for budgets
explain: Transparency supports sustainable relationships.
level: 1

Q: The biggest risk to a small business’s cash should be:
Ignored
*Identified and reduced with practical steps
Celebrated

explain: Risk management is part of good money practice.
level: 1

Q: A monthly money review is useful because:
It replaces all daily tracking
*It keeps goals and plans aligned with reality
It is required only for banks
It increases taxes automatically
explain: Regular review drives continuous improvement.
level: 2

Q: Diversifying income sources over time mainly helps:
Concentrate all risk in one place
*Reduce dependence on a single source
Eliminate the need for savings

explain: Multiple sources improve resilience.
level: 2

Q: When tax rules are unclear the best immediate step is:
Ignore them completely
*Seek reliable information or qualified advice
Guess the highest possible amount

explain: Accurate information prevents larger problems.
level: 2

Q: Choosing growth investments should consider:
Only what looks exciting
*Expected return and risk relative to other uses of the money
Only what competitors are doing

explain: Opportunity cost and risk matter.
level: 2

Q: The overall aim of this course is to help you:
Memorise complex accounting standards
*Manage money more confidently from basic tracking through to planning and growth
Avoid all formal systems forever
Replace professional accountants in every case
explain: Practical confidence across the money cycle is the goal.
level: 1
